claim: Plasmodium falciparum is responsible for the most virulent form of malaria

claim: P. falciparum merozoites invade erythrocytes
source: Merozoites of the protozoan parasite responsible for the most virulent form of malaria, Plasmodium falciparum, invade erythrocytes.

claim: Invasion involves discharge of rhoptries, specialized secretory organelles
source: Invasion involves discharge of rhoptries, specialized secretory organelles.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: Intracellular parasites induce increased nutrient uptake by generating new permeability pathways (NPP) including a Plasmodium surface anion channel (PSAC)
source: Once intracellular, parasites induce increased nutrient uptake by generating new permeability pathways (NPP) including a Plasmodium surface anion channel (PSAC).

claim: RhopH1/Clag3 is important for PSAC/NPP activity

claim: The roles of other members of the RhopH complex in PSAC/NPP establishment are unknown

claim: RhopH3 is essential for parasite survival

claim: Conditional truncation of RhopH3 substantially reduces invasive capacity
source: Conditional truncation of RhopH3 substantially reduces invasive capacity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by invasion assays showing ~50% reduction

claim: Mutant parasites that invade are defective in nutrient import and die
source: Those mutant parasites that do invade are defective in nutrient import and die.

claim: RhopH3 has a dual role that links erythrocyte invasion to formation of the PSAC/NPP essential for parasite survival
source: Our results identify a dual role for RhopH3 that links erythrocyte invasion to formation of the PSAC/NPP essential for parasite survival within host erythrocytes.

claim: Malaria claims nearly 600,000 lives each year
source: Parasites of the genus Plasmodium are the causative agents of malaria, a disease that claims nearly 600,000 lives each year (WHO, 2014).

claim: P. falciparum is responsible for nearly all the mortality associated with malaria
source: Of the five Plasmodium species that infect humans, Plasmodium falciparum is responsible for nearly all the mortality associated with malaria.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge

claim: The P. falciparum intraerythrocytic life cycle is approximately 48 hours
source: For approximately the first half of the 48 hour P. falciparum intraerythrocytic life cycle, the parasite exists in a mononuclear trophozoite form

claim: P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes gain the capacity to adhere to host vascular endothelium during the trophozoite phase
source: During this phase, P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes gain the capacity to adhere to host vascular endothelium, a process that depends on the export of parasite proteins to form adhesive structures called knobs at the host erythrocyte surface.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about parasite biology

claim: Adhesion to host vascular endothelium depends on the export of parasite proteins to form adhesive structures called knobs at the host erythrocyte surface
source: During this phase, P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes gain the capacity to adhere to host vascular endothelium, a process that depends on the export of parasite proteins to form adhesive structures called knobs at the host erythrocyte surface.

claim: Rhoptries are thought to mediate formation of the nascent parasitophorous vacuole (PV)

evidence: This is cited from previous literature

claim: Rhoptries comprise at least two subdomains referred to as the rhoptry neck and the rhoptry bulb
source: Rhoptries comprise at least two subdomains (Counihan et al., 2013) referred to as the rhoptry neck and the rhoptry bulb.

claim: The contents of rhoptry neck and rhoptry bulb subdomains likely mediate different functions

claim: Proteins of the rhoptry neck are well conserved between Plasmodium spp. and Toxoplasma gondii
source: Proteins of the rhoptry neck are well conserved between Plasmodium spp. and the related apicomplexan parasite Toxoplasma gondii, suggesting conserved functions (Counihan et al., 2013; Proellocks et al., 2010).

claim: Proteins of the rhoptry bulb appear to be genus-specific

claim: The RhopH complex consists of three proteins called RhopH1/Clag, RhopH2, and RhopH3
source: One component of the P. falciparum rhoptry bulb that has received particular attention is the so-called high molecular weight (HMW) rhoptry or RhopH complex, which consists of three proteins called RhopH1/Clag, RhopH2, and RhopH3 (Cooper et al., 1988; Holder et al., 1985a).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature

claim: RhopH2 and RhopH3 are each encoded by single-copy genes
source: Whilst RhopH2 and RhopH3 are each encoded by single-copy genes, RhopH1/Clag, the largest component of the complex, exists in five isotypes encoded by separate genes entitled clag2, clag3.1, clag3.2, clag8 and clag9 (Kaneko et al., 2001, 2005).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature

claim: RhopH1/Clag exists in five isotypes encoded by separate genes entitled clag2, clag3.1, clag3.2, clag8 and clag9
source: Whilst RhopH2 and RhopH3 are each encoded by single-copy genes, RhopH1/Clag, the largest component of the complex, exists in five isotypes encoded by separate genes entitled clag2, clag3.1, clag3.2, clag8 and clag9 (Kaneko et al., 2001, 2005).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature

claim: RhopH1/Clag3.1 and RhopH1/Clag3.2 are nearly identical proteins that are expressed in a mutually exclusive manner
source: RhopH1/Clag3.1 and RhopH1/Clag3.2 are nearly identical proteins that are expressed in a mutually exclusive manner (Chung et al., 2007; Comeaux et al., 2011; Cortés et al., 2007).

claim: Each RhopH complex contains only one form of RhopH1/Clag
source: Each RhopH complex contains only one form of RhopH1/Clag (Kaneko et al., 2005), so each parasite has the potential to produce four different RhopH complexes, differentiated by the particular RhopH1/Clag isotype bound.

claim: All members of the RhopH complex are expressed late in the intraerythrocytic cycle
source: All members of the RhopH complex are expressed late in the intraerythrocytic cycle (Cooper et al., 1988).

claim: The RhopH complex is released during invasion
source: The complex is then released during invasion (Ling et al., 2003) and inserted into the nascent PV membrane (PVM) soon after parasite entry (Ling et al., 2004; Sam-Yellowe et al., 1988).

claim: The RhopH complex is inserted into the nascent PV membrane (PVM) soon after parasite entry
source: The complex is then released during invasion (Ling et al., 2003) and inserted into the nascent PV membrane (PVM) soon after parasite entry (Ling et al., 2004; Sam-Yellowe et al., 1988).

claim: RhopH1/Clag3 proteins have a role in the function of the Plasmodium surface anion channel (PSAC)
source: Genetic and chemical genetic investigation has revealed a role for the RhopH1/Clag3 proteins in the function of the Plasmodium surface anion channel (PSAC), a new permeability pathway (NPP) induced in host erythrocytes following parasite entry and involved in nutrient acquisition by the intracellular parasite (Nguitragool et al., 2011).

claim: Part of the RhopH1/Clag3.2 protein is exposed at the surface of the erythrocyte
source: Pharmacological inhibition of RhopH1/Clag3.2 function was found to block PSAC/NPP activity, and selection for drug-resistant mutants revealed that part of the protein is exposed at the surface of the erythrocyte and that it may form the channel itself (Nguitragool et al., 2014; Sharma et al., 2015).

claim: RhopH1/Clag3.2 may form the PSAC channel itself

evidence: This is cited from previous literature with speculative language ('may form')

claim: Parasites that do not produce either RhopH1/Clag3.1 or RhopH1/Clag3.2 display only a small growth disadvantage

claim: Inhibition of RhopH1/Clag3 function has only a small effect on parasite growth rates in vitro
